title: Merge the Piles of Stones k at a Time

concept.title: Merging k piles at a time: count how many piles are left in a range
body: Piles of stones stand in a row. In one move you take **exactly `k` consecutive piles** and merge them into one pile; the move costs the total number of stones in those `k` piles. You repeat until a single pile is left. What is the smallest total cost? For the piles `3 2 4 1` and `k = 2` the answer is 20; for `3 2 4 1` and `k = 3` it is impossible: -1. A pile count `n` can be reduced to 1 only if `(n - 1)` is divisible by `(k - 1)`, because every move removes `k - 1` piles.

Let `cost(i, j)` be the smallest cost of merging the piles `i .. j` into **as few piles as possible**, which is 1 pile if `(j - i)` is divisible by `k - 1`, and otherwise a larger number that cannot be merged further inside the range. Any such state can be split: the first pile of the final state of the range covers the piles `i .. m`, and the rest of the range is merged independently. So **`cost(i, j) = min over m of cost(i, m) + cost(m + 1, j)`** where `m` goes `i, i + (k - 1), i + 2(k - 1), ...` (the left part must be one complete pile). If the range `i .. j` can become exactly **one pile**, one last merge of `k` piles is added, and it costs the sum of the whole range: `+ sum(i .. j)`.

Stepping `m` by `k - 1` keeps the left part a single pile, so each range is split in about `length / (k - 1)` ways. Total time O(n^3 / (k - 1)) and memory O(n^2). The ideas to take: when the number of objects left in a range matters, make it a part of the state, or use the arithmetic (here divisibility by `k - 1`) to keep it implicit.

statement: `n` piles of stones stand in a row. In one move you merge exactly `k` consecutive piles into one pile; the cost of the move is the total number of stones in the merged piles. Print the smallest total cost of merging all piles into one, or -1 if it is impossible.
inputFormat: The first line has `n` and `k`: the number of piles and the number of piles merged at a time.
The second line has `n` numbers: the number of stones in each pile.
outputFormat: Print the smallest total cost, or -1.

examples.note: Four piles cannot be merged three at a time into one: -1.

hints: If (n - 1) is not divisible by (k - 1), the answer is -1.
cost(i, j) = the minimum of cost(i, m) + cost(m + 1, j) over m = i, i + (k - 1), ...
If the range can become one pile ((j - i) divisible by k - 1), add the sum of the range for the last merge.

starter.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n, k = map(int, input().split())
piles = list(map(int, input().split()))

explanation: If n - 1 is not divisible by k - 1 the answer is -1. Otherwise cost(i, j) is the smallest cost to merge the piles i to j as far as possible: the minimum over the split m = i, i + (k - 1), ... of cost(i, m) + cost(m + 1, j), plus the sum of the range when it can become a single pile. The answer is cost(0, n - 1).
